channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: AAA forecasts slight drop in Thanksgiving travel, in part due to higher costs
item.description:
Source: Washington Post
AAA forecasts a slight decrease in Thanksgiving travel, with 81.5 million Americans expected to travel, down from last year’s 81.6 million but above the 2024 peak of 80.2 million. The majority of trips, 72.9 million, will be by car, down 200,000 from last year due to high gas prices, while 6 million will fly. AAA Travel’s Vice President Stacey Barber attributed the drop to higher travel costs, noting that volumes remain near record levels. A ground stop causing flight cancellations earlier in the week did not significantly impact the forecast, according to AAA spokesperson Aixa Diaz, who said holiday travelers are unlikely to be deterred by such disruptions.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise to 7.34% Amid Fed Hike Anticipation
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Tuesday, November 17: A Little Higher
Mortgage rates rose to 7.34% APR for a 30-year fixed loan, up seven basis points from yesterday and 34 basis points from a week ago. The increase follows anticipation of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December to curb inflation. The Producer Price Index showed mixed inflation data: 0.3% month-over-month (vs. 0.4% expected) and 6.5% year-over-year, the highest in four years. Higher inflation pressures suggest future consumer costs will rise. Investors expect the Fed to raise the federal funds rate, which influences mortgage rates. Homeowners are advised to consider refinancing if current rates are 0.5-0.75% lower than their existing rate, though timing depends on individual financial goals. Rate locks are recommended to protect against market fluctuations. Advertised rates differ from personalized quotes due to factors like credit scores, down payments, and financial profiles. Lenders adjust rates frequently, so quotes can change until locked. Preapproval and budgeting are emphasized for potential buyers.

item.title: Russia Demands NATO Roll Back to 1997
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
Russia presented a document during Ukraine war talks in Abu Dhabi, demanding NATO end military presence in Eastern Europe and roll back to 1997 levels. The 1997 reference points to NATO's pre-eastward expansion state, with 16 members. Russia does not explicitly demand Eastern European countries leave NATO but seeks to end the alliance's military presence there. A withdrawal would weaken defense for Baltic states and Romania, where a major NATO air base is under construction. NATO members Poland, Bulgaria, and Estonia reject Russian demands, emphasizing their security arrangements. The mutual-defense clause's effectiveness relies on NATO's military presence. Past agreements like the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the 1994 Budapest Memorandum did not legally bind NATO to stop expansion. Russia's demands, part of its strategy to address 'root causes' of the war, face rejection from Western allies, who view the talks as an attempt to delay confrontation.

item.title: TSA Warns of Thanksgiving Travel Chaos, Advises Preparations
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: TSA addressing Thanksgiving travel ahead of busy holiday travel season
TSA warns of Thanksgiving travel chaos, advising travelers to prepare for high volumes. Jessica Mayle, TSA Regional Spokesperson, said Friday and Saturday will be busy days in San Diego, urging passengers to pack smart and avoid prohibited items. San Diego International Airport expects nearly a million passengers from November 23-30, a 8-10% increase, with 87,000 daily travelers. TSA emphasized readiness for disruptions, like recent FAA ground stops and United system issues, by adjusting staffing, using canine teams, and overtime. Officials urged travelers to plan ahead, check allowed items, carry proper ID, and arrive early. Nicole Hall of the airport echoed TSA’s coordination with airlines and federal partners to ensure smooth holiday travel.

item.title: Mullin Testifies on Ground Stop and Tech Issues
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: Mullin faces congressional hearing in the wake of historic nationwide ground stop
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin will testify before a House Committee hearing on Wednesday about worldwide threats since Sept. 11, 2001. The focus will include questions about a nationwide ground stop that stranded millions of passengers last weekend. The disruption, caused by a Juniper router installation in Arkansas, overwhelmed an outdated copper wire system, leading to telecommunications failures. Mullin and other officials will face scrutiny over the FAA's use of 50-year-old equipment and the 69th router installation that triggered the incident. Mullin told CNBC the FAA's issues stem from outdated copper infrastructure, not cyberattacks, and emphasized the homeland is secure. He also defended his attendance at a college football game despite ongoing flight disruptions, stating he would not have flown if airways were closed. The hearing will also address cyber outages affecting airlines, Microsoft Outlook, and banks.

item.title: EU and ASEAN Seek Closer Trade Ties Amid Informal Barriers
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain as businesses struggle with informal barriers
The European Union and ASEAN aim to deepen trade ties ahead of their 50th anniversary in 2027. Progress includes pending trade deals with Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand, and Malaysia, potentially expanding EU FTAs from two to six Southeast Asian states. However, challenges persist beyond tariff reductions, as businesses face informal barriers. Chris Humphrey of the EU-ASEAN Business Council emphasized that FTAs are only the start, stressing the need for communication and training to help companies navigate local practices. European firms require support in market entry, regulatory clarity, and understanding unwritten business rules. Alfred Gerstl highlighted the importance of expanding European chambers of commerce assistance, citing examples like improved access for pharmaceutical firms in Vietnam and trade facilitation in Indonesia. Political and geopolitical factors also play a role, with the EU seeking to reduce mineral dependencies while Southeast Asian nations want foreign investment in processing industries. Pending EU-Singapore and EU-Vietnam investment agreements remain unratified, delaying their implementation. Debate continues over whether to pursue bilateral deals or revive a region-wide FTA, with Humphrey advocating for a Digital Trade Agreement and common standards. The 2027 anniversary could mark a turning point, but experts warn against treating diplomatic events as progress without concrete action.

item.title: UK inflation hits one-year high of 3.6% in October
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: UK inflation rose to one-year high of 3.6% in October
UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October, the highest in a year, driven by petrol prices and other factors. The Office for National Statistics reported the increase, surpassing September’s 3.5% and aligning with economists’ forecasts. Petrol prices hit their highest since August 2022, while software, books, and package holidays also contributed. Inflation has exceeded the Bank of England’s 2% target for over two years, with energy costs from the Middle East war expected to push prices higher. The BoE raised rates to 4% this month and signaled further hikes, anticipating inflation peaking at 5% next year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces pressure after announcing a £100 energy handout. Services inflation remained at 3.7%, core inflation stayed at 2.8%, and food prices eased. Economists are divided on timing for future rate hikes, with some predicting a December increase. Traders estimate an 80% chance of a quarter-point rise in December, though analysts like Lee Hardman question if energy costs will broaden inflation pressures. The pound fell 0.4% against the dollar. Felix Feather noted October’s rise may not prompt immediate action but emphasized the meeting remains open. Huw Pill, the BoE’s chief economist, expects a quarter-point increase in December and further rises in 2024.

item.title: EU to use Russian frozen asset profits for Ukraine loan
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Brussels to tap Russian frozen asset profits to service new Ukraine loan
The European Commission will propose using profits from frozen Russian assets to service a new €45bn loan to Ukraine, part of efforts to address a €70bn funding gap for 2027. The plan includes repaying third countries’ loans from Russia’s asset profits, which currently fund a €45bn loan from G7 partners. The EU aims to secure full member state consent for the €45bn loan, avoiding opt-outs from Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic. About €25bn will target defense, with rules favoring European and Ukrainian manufacturers, while €20bn supports broader needs. The proposal extends frozen asset profits to repay existing and new loans. The Commission also seeks guarantees from non-EU G7 countries like Canada and Australia for additional €5bn. The plan follows a 2023 agreement to raise €90bn for Ukraine, with the new loan to be funded from the bloc’s current budget.

item.title: Ukraine Destroys Crimean Bridge's Main Span in Major Strike
item.description:
Source: BBC News, NYT World News Original headline: Ukraine Destroys Key Section of Crimean Bridge in Major Strike
Ukraine destroyed a critical section of the Crimean Bridge in a seven-stage operation using drones and missiles, including a modified Flamingo missile. The 12-mile-long bridge, a symbol of Russia's control over Crimea since 2014, suffered catastrophic damage when its 227-meter main road arch collapsed into the Black Sea. Footage from the Flamingo missile's onboard camera showed the attack on the steel arches, confirmed by munitions expert Justin Bronk. The strike followed a preliminary attack on November 16 that damaged but did not disable the bridge. The final assault occurred on November 17, two days before Russian President Vladimir Putin's planned summit with U.S. and Chinese leaders. Russian officials confirmed the damage and vowed to rebuild the bridge, calling it 'even better than before.' Structural engineers described the collapse as rendering the bridge inoperable for over a year. Ukraine's attack, its most significant strike on the bridge, targets Russia's supply line to Crimea. Zelensky cited recent Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure as justification. The bridge, costing Russia $4 billion, was heavily fortified with air defenses and electronic systems.

item.title: Russia Imports Record Petrol Amid Refinery Damage from Ukraine
item.description:
Source: Business Insider, FT World Original headline: Russia's Petrol Crisis Deepens as Imports Surge Amid Ukrainian Attacks on Refineries
Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have damaged key refineries, reducing total refinery capacity by 55% and forcing Russia to rely on petrol imports. The country has shifted from a major fuel exporter to a significant importer, with record volumes of petrol arriving by sea and rail. Analysts call this a 'remarkable reversal' of Russia's traditional role. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak acknowledged the crisis, urging agencies to prioritize expanding petrol imports and securing lower-grade fuel, typically reserved for exports or military use. International data shows Russia imported over 416,000 metric tons of petrol by sea in August, with another 234,000 metric tons arriving in September. Belarusian refineries supplied over 600,000 metric tons since July, while Kazakhstan added 8,000 metric tons. Local officials in six Russian regions implemented gasoline rationing, capping daily purchases at 30 liters. Russia's petrol production remains 13-18% below 2026 levels. Novak stated Russia would continue importing fuel until year-end to address shortages. Ukraine’s GUR estimates Russia has imported nearly 1 million metric tons of fuel by sea since July, marking a dramatic shift from exporter to importer.

item.title: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents
item.description:
Source: Business Insider
Amazon blocked external AI shopping agents like Muse and Instinct from making purchases, citing security and customer experience concerns. CEO Andy Jassy said the company hasn't ruled out future openness, emphasizing the need for a 'good customer experience' and 'fair exchange of value.' AI agents, including Meta's Muse, Instinct AI, and OpenAI's Dots, pose challenges for retailers by potentially bypassing traditional browsing controls and raising issues around ad sales, account security, and liability. Amazon is advancing its own AI tools, such as Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me, which leverage customer data for personalized purchases. Jassy argued that users would prefer agentic shopping tools aligned with their preferred retailers, citing the convenience of accessing past orders and payment info. Shopify has embraced external agents, while Home Depot's CIO mentioned the need for agents to self-identify on its platform. Amazon maintains its policies apply evenly, though users report struggles with third-party agents on its site.

item.title: Nvidia Board Rejects Jensen Huang's Return as CEO
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: Transcript: Nvidia board insists Huang won’t return as CEO
Nvidia's board confirmed it will not reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO following his resignation amid allegations of misconduct. The company reported strong financial results, including doubled sales in the latest quarter and a revised 2025 sales forecast. During the earnings call, the board emphasized business continuity under interim CEO Colette Kress, who also serves as CFO. They avoided discussing Huang’s resignation, focusing instead on financial performance and succession planning. The stock rose in after-hours trading despite ongoing regulatory uncertainties, including potential scrutiny over Huang’s alleged affairs and export compliance issues. The board established a national security and export oversight committee to address these concerns. Meanwhile, analysts predict a slowdown in global earnings growth next year, with S&P 500 profits expected to drop from 36% to 11% annually. Despite this, investors remain optimistic about market resilience, citing undervalued tech stocks and potential regional convergence in earnings growth.

item.title: Nvidia Establishes National Security Committee Following Huang Resignation
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
Nvidia announced the creation of a board-level National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down after admitting to extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and allegedly facilitating the export of advanced chips to the country. The scandal has intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in US national security and contributed to a 28% decline in its stock price over a month. The new committee, chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson, will meet quarterly and include legal and compliance experts. It will oversee existing teams focused on national security and trade compliance. Board Chair Harvey Jones emphasized collaboration with government and industry to balance security with innovation. US President Donald Trump praised the move, though he previously advocated for relaxed export controls to China. Intelligence reports suggest suspicions about Huang's affairs and ties to Chinese intelligence were known for over a year.

item.title: Apple Resolves Service Outages Amid Recent Tech Disruptions
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Apple Addresses Outages Affecting Apple Pay, iCloud and Apps
Apple resolved service outages affecting Apple Pay, iCloud, and apps after an internal update disrupted systems on Tuesday. The company reported all systems were restored by early evening. The outage followed unrelated glitches at JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft, and United Airlines, as well as a FAA ground stop due to outdated air traffic equipment. Chetrice Romero, a cybersecurity adviser, noted the recent string of outages highlights reliance on technology and warned of scams exploiting the disruptions. She emphasized banks won’t request sensitive information via text. JPMorgan attributed its outage to a software bug, while Microsoft’s outage was linked to a technical issue. Banking networks’ interconnectedness caused cascading effects, with some banks reporting issues. The FAA’s ground stop followed a router upgrade at a radio facility. All major outages were resolved within hours, though they raised concerns about system resilience.

item.title: UK October Inflation Remains Energy-Driven, Core Stable
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: UK’s October inflation rise remains largely energy related
UK headline inflation rose to 3.6% in October, matching expectations but slightly below Bank of England forecasts. Core inflation remained steady at 2.8%, with services inflation holding at 3.7%. Energy costs, particularly diesel prices at 199.5p per litre, drove the increase, contributing 0.12 percentage points. Alcohol and tobacco duty timing added 0.06 percentage points, while recreation and culture costs added 0.05. Food inflation slowed to 0.9%, and housing costs stayed at 5.3%. Services inflation showed no acceleration, with energy-related transport costs being the main factor. The BoE faces a tight decision on December rate hikes, balancing the need to prevent persistent inflation against managing interest rate expectations. While underlying inflation risks remain elevated, the central bank is likely to adopt a gradual tightening path, potentially skipping a December rate increase.

item.title: Recent Tech Outages Linked to System Updates and AI-Driven Vulnerabilities
item.description:
Source: Vox Original headline: When do we start worrying about all these outages?
Recent widespread tech outages, including Microsoft Outlook, air traffic control, bank systems, Apple, and NSA communications, have raised concerns about system reliability. Most issues were not caused by cyberattacks but technical glitches. Lily Hay Newman, WIRED's senior writer, explained that Microsoft's prolonged Outlook outage stemmed from a flawed Windows update that spread through its infrastructure for three months. The update's flaw, combined with complex cloud infrastructure, delayed resolution. Newman also discussed the 'vulnepocalypse'—a surge in software vulnerabilities exacerbated by AI's ability to rapidly identify and exploit bugs. Recent events like Black October, which saw critical PHP vulnerabilities, and the $6 billion Binance hack by North Korean actors, highlight ongoing systemic risks. Newman noted that while the current outage wave feels unprecedented, it aligns with cyclical patterns of tech failures, citing past DDoS attacks and East Coast internet outages. She emphasized that while AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and exploitation, such incidents are not new, though they are becoming more frequent and complex.

item.title: Tech Outages Disrupt Travel, Banking; Officials Rule Out Cyberattacks
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: A string of tech outages disrupted flights, banking, and major apps. Here's what officials have said about the causes.
A series of technology outages disrupted travel, banking, and major apps, prompting officials to address potential causes. The Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights for over four hours due to air traffic control system issues, with officials blaming aging infrastructure. Microsoft reported a technical outage affecting its 365 suite, while JPMorgan Chase cited a software bug in on-premise hardware. United Airlines resolved a 'technology issue' causing flight delays, and Charles Schwab and Apple attributed outages to internal updates and server misconfigurations. Sen. Mark Warner stated there's no evidence of cyberattacks or AI involvement, noting AI's role in identifying vulnerabilities has increased pressure on outdated systems. Officials from the Department of Transportation and Homeland Security emphasized the outages were not linked to cybersecurity threats. All affected companies denied cyberattack involvement, citing technical or infrastructure issues as the root causes.

item.title: Nvidia Board Rejects Reinstatement of Jensen Huang Amid Security Concerns
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Business, BBC News, Business Insider, NYT > Business, San Diego Union-Tribune, FT World Original headline: Nvidia Board Rejects Reinstatement of Former CEO Jensen Huang Amid Financial Success and National Security Scrutiny
Nvidia's board has rejected calls to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned in November over allegations of personal misconduct, including an affair with a woman linked to Chinese intelligence. Board chair Harvey Jones stated during an earnings call that the company 'does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO' following his 'voluntary resignation' for 'personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct.' Huang expressed willingness to return if deemed beneficial, but the board emphasized adherence to national security policies and U.S. export controls. The board formed a committee to oversee these areas amid concerns over the company's role in global trade and technology risks. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter, doubling from the prior year, and profits surged to $65.3 billion. Shares rose 4.8% but remain below pre-Huang levels, with a $573 billion market value loss since the scandal. The company halted H200 chip shipments to China after months of lobbying by Huang. U.S. lawmakers and intelligence officials are investigating his alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman and an employee. Nvidia launched an independent probe, while Huang apologized for 'serious mistakes in personal life.' Shareholder petitions for reinstatement have gained traction, but the board has not indicated reconsideration. Interim CEO Colette Kress highlighted the company's resilience, while the board seeks a permanent CEO amid ongoing scrutiny.
item.source: NPR Topics: Business, BBC News, Business Insider, NYT > Business, San Diego Union-Tribune, FT World

item.title: San Diego Economy Outpaces Southern California in 2027
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Report: San Diego economy outpaces much of SoCal
San Diego County's economy grew 0.9% in 2026, outperforming Los Angeles and Orange County. BMO reports businesses prioritize automation and efficiency over hiring, with aerospace, healthcare, AI infrastructure, and utilities as growth areas. Consumer spending remains resilient among high-income households, but import-dependent sectors face tariffs and rising costs. Home prices rose 6.3%, the strongest gain in Southern California, driven by limited inventory and low mortgage rates. Building permits hit 20% above 2025 levels, though higher construction costs persist. Companies focus on retaining talent and selective hiring, while financing and M&A activity increase despite valuation gaps. Data centers face grid capacity and permitting hurdles. Risks include inflation, trade uncertainty, labor shortages, and housing affordability. The report forecasts moderate growth in 2027, citing resilient housing demand and employment gains in key sectors despite industry-specific challenges.

item.title: Gen Z managers to surpass baby boomers by 2027
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Gen Z managers could outnumber baby boomers as soon as 2027
A new report from job sites Indeed and Glassdoor predicts Gen Z will surpass baby boomers in management roles by 2027 and overtake Gen X by 2,033. The report states Gen Z now constitutes 12% of managers, up from 12% of the labor force. Laura Ullrich, director of economic research at Indeed Hiring Lab, noted Gen Z's positivity despite challenges, with survey data showing greater optimism about career success compared to older generations. Millennials still hold 38% of managerial roles, though generational differences persist, such as preference for remote work. The report highlights a mentorship gap, with 58% of Gen Zers seeking mentors but only 25% receiving them. Ben Whybrow, a 22-year-old in the UK, transitioned to management without adequate support, later returning to a non-managerial role. He expressed frustration with limited support networks for young managers but remains eager to lead with more guidance.

item.title: Voyager 1 Breaks Cosmic Distance Record
item.description:
Source: Vox, The Atlantic
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, will cross 16 billion miles from Earth tomorrow, marking the first time a human-made object reaches that distance. This point, one light-day from Earth, remains within the solar system. Scientists use light-years to measure such distances, with Alpha Centauri at 4.5 light-years. Voyager 1, which transmitted data from interstellar space since 2012, will lose power to its transmitter by 2030 but will continue drifting for billions of years. Originally designed for a 'Grand Tour' of the outer planets, the spacecraft completed its primary mission and crossed the heliopause in 2012. Both Voyager 1 and 2 carry the Golden Record, a gold-plated disc with sounds, images, and messages in 55 languages, though some content was excluded due to rights issues or NASA objections. Notable exclusions include the Beatles' 'Here Comes the Sun' and explicit imagery. The spacecraft now serve as distant sentinels, carrying humanity's message into the cosmos.

item.title: Gen Z Embraces Winter Challenges, Struggles With Financial Goals
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Survey: Gen Z Loves a Winter Challenge, but Money Goals Often Fizzle
A NerdWallet survey by The Harris Poll reveals Gen Zers are most likely to engage in winter self-improvement challenges but struggle to complete them. 74% of Gen Zers (ages 18-29) have tried a winter challenge, compared to 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers, and 29% of baby boomers. However, 59% of Gen Zers quit challenges before finishing, versus 42% of millennials and 22% of baby boomers. Financial goals are particularly challenging: 64% of Gen Zers say sticking to past financial goals was hard, and 33% set the same goal multiple times. Despite efforts, 90% of Gen Zers expect higher winter discretionary spending, with food delivery, entertainment, and fitness apps as top expenses. 26% bought products seen on social media for goals, and 60% delay financial tasks until after the holidays. Personal finance expert Kimberly Palmer advises aligning challenges with long-term goals and seeking support to improve success rates.

item.title: Myanmar Genocide Case at World Court to Be Ruled
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: What to Know About the Myanmar Genocide Case at the World Court
The International Court of Justice will rule Thursday on whether Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims, a case brought by Gambia in 2019 with support from 11 countries. The U.S. has already classified Myanmar’s 2017 violence against Rohingya as genocide, involving mass killings, sexual violence, and arson. A guilty verdict would mark the first time a state is held accountable under the 1948 Genocide Convention, potentially influencing other cases like South Africa’s claim against Israel. Rohingya, rendered stateless since 1982, faced systematic persecution, including village burnings and forced displacement, leading to 1.2 million refugees in Bangladesh. The court’s definition of genocide requires intent to destroy a group, a standard critics say is hard to prove. Survivors like Mohammed Furkhan describe the violence as an effort to erase their people. A guilty verdict could set legal precedents for reparations but may lack enforcement power due to China and Russia’s influence. The International Criminal Court separately investigates individual perpetrators, including Myanmar’s former military chief.

item.title: California Faces Another Storm with Heavy Rain and Snow
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Another Storm Is Bearing Down on California
A new storm system is hitting California with heavy rain, snow, and strong winds, continuing a series of intense weather events. The storm, arriving amid a strong El Niño, is expected to bring 2 to 6 inches of rain along the coast, with 2.5 inches in San Francisco. Flooding risks are heightened by elevated sea levels and high tides. The storm will also deliver the first significant snowfall of the season, with up to five feet possible on Sierra Nevada peaks. Meteorologists warn of wind gusts up to 70 mph, potential power outages, and travel disruptions. The storm will exit by early Friday, but another is expected by Sunday, with a possible Thanksgiving storm posing a risk during high tides. 'It’s definitely going to be chillier,' said Scott Kleebauer. 'The storm will likely be one of the better snowpack contributors,' added Chad Hecht.

item.title: Job Seekers Use Quirky Tactics to Stand Out Amid AI Resumes
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Welcome to the 'screw-it' job market
Amanda McDormand, a 43-year-old job seeker, used unconventional cover letters featuring Taylor Swift lyrics and pop culture references to stand out in a market flooded with AI-generated applications. Her strategies, including golf jokes and direct pitches, led to callbacks and a full-time role. Over 84% of job seekers now use AI to craft resumes, prompting candidates to adopt creative tactics like adding quirky hobbies or personal anecdotes to signal humanity. Recruiters report receiving an average of 194 applications per hire, making it harder to differentiate. Marc Cenedella of Ladders notes that 76% of job seekers intentionally sound less like AI. Some applicants embrace bold moves, like sharing sob stories or niche interests, to cut through resume fatigue. While some hiring managers appreciate the creativity, others warn that overly eccentric details could backfire. Erica Keswin advises against generic stunts, emphasizing authenticity. McDormand’s approach, blending pop culture with strategic storytelling, highlights the balance between creativity and professionalism in a competitive job market.

item.title: Wall Street Forecasts Global Earnings Growth to Halve Next Year
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Wall Street expects corporate earnings growth to halve next year
Wall Street analysts predict global corporate earnings growth will drop to 16% in 2027 from 33.5% this year, driven by slowing AI capital expenditure. Goldman Sachs’ Peter Oppenheimer forecasts a more than halving of earnings growth across major markets, with U.S. profits falling to 11% and Europe to 7%. The slowdown stems from cooling AI investment growth, which is expected to peak in early 2027, and rising depreciation costs for physical AI assets. Global AI capex is projected to rise from $1.1tn in 2026 to $1.8tn in 2027, but at a slower pace. Barclays expects U.S. earnings growth to decline to 15% from over 30%, while Asia-Pacific ex-Japan’s growth will fall from 74% to 26%. Despite the slowdown, analysts still anticipate the S&P 500 to rise 9% next year, citing lower valuations. Oppenheimer calls U.S. equities attractive relative to other markets. In Europe, energy sector earnings will slow as oil prices are expected to drop to $78/barrel by 2027. Morgan Stanley’s Marina Zavolock notes EU equities are narrowing valuation gaps with U.S. peers, signaling a shift from U.S. dominance in global markets.

item.title: Putin Open to Meeting North Korea's Leader at APEC Summit in China
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Putin Is Open to Meeting With North Korea’s Leader in China, Kremlin Says
Putin is open to meeting North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen if Kim attends, the Kremlin said. Kremlin spokesman Dmitri Peskov confirmed the meeting would occur if Kim travels to China. North Korea has supported Russia’s actions in Ukraine, and the two leaders have met three times since 2022. The APEC summit will also host a trilateral meeting between Putin, China’s Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Trump, marking the first such gathering. Putin emphasized North Korea’s role in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region last year, calling it a new chapter in military cooperation. Moscow plans to unveil a monument in Kursk honoring North Korean troops by year’s end. Kim’s potential attendance would be his first trip outside North Korea in years and could lead to a meeting with Trump.

item.title: Tick Bites Linked to Meat Allergy, Scientists Find
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: From tick bite to meat allergy: Scientists investigate the mystery link
Sandra Tiguila developed a meat allergy after tick bites, leading to alpha-gal syndrome. The condition, linked to a sugar molecule in red meat, causes severe reactions ranging from rashes to anaphylaxis. Researchers, including Onyinye Iweala and Maya Jerath, found that tick bites trigger the immune system to react to alpha-gal. Studies connected the syndrome to cetuximab drug reactions and tick exposure, with the lone star tick being a major culprit in the U.S. The CDC estimates up to 450,000 people may be affected since 2010. Scientists discovered that alpha-gal antibodies rise after tick bites, with exposure via skin rather than gut reducing tolerance. Treatments include antihistamines, EpiPens, and avoiding mammal products. Tiguila’s allergy reversed after her IgE levels dropped. Researchers still seek to understand why some ticks cause the allergy while others don’t, and why some people develop it without tick bites.

item.title: Sixth Central Coast E. coli case linked to toddler's death
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Sixth Central Coast resident confirmed with E. coli, nearly a week after a bacteria-related death
A sixth Central Coast resident has been diagnosed with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, linked to a larger outbreak that killed an 18-month-old girl. The infected individual, identified at a preschool in San Luis Obispo, was exposed through person-to-person transmission from previously confirmed cases. Officials have not released details about the school or the infected person. The outbreak, connected to Brookshire Farms, resulted in 15 infections, five confirmed, with three children requiring intensive care. Genetic testing of five confirmed cases showed a common strain not found in national databases, suggesting a unique source. Environmental samples from the farm did not detect STEC, though other E. coli strains were present. Hemolytic uremic syndrome, a severe complication, occurred in one case, with the affected child recovering at home. State data shows STEC infections in California rose from 500 in 2011 to over 2,500 in 2023.

item.title: US-backed railway aims to boost DR Congo's mineral exports and regional stability
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
The Lobito Corridor, a US-backed railway linking DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast, aims to boost critical mineral exports and regional economic cooperation. The project, part of a Trump-era agreement between DR Congo and Rwanda, seeks to formalize mineral trade, reduce reliance on China, and curb illicit markets funding armed groups. The railway, rebuilt in 2015, now transports copper and cobalt to global markets, with plans to increase cargo to 200,000 tonnes by 2026. Local benefits include cheaper travel and jobs, with over 1,000 Angolan workers employed. However, challenges remain, including conflict in eastern DR Congo, where mineral wealth fuels instability, and debates over whether the corridor should prioritize raw material exports or local processing. Analysts argue the project's success depends on infrastructure upgrades, regional investment, and ensuring mineral wealth benefits local economies rather than external markets. DR Congo's Economy Minister urged the US to focus on tangible projects, not just agreements, to achieve peace and development.

item.title: Intel cuts more jobs as CEO Tan's restructuring continues
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Intel cuts more jobs as CEO Lip-Bu Tan's efficiency push continues
Intel has announced another round of layoffs as part of CEO Lip-Bu Tan's ongoing restructuring efforts. Employees in the global IT workforce reported job cuts this week, with the company stating it is aligning resources with priorities. Intel did not specify the number of affected employees or teams. The cuts continue a years-long restructuring aimed at reviving the chipmaker after manufacturing setbacks and losing market share in AI chips. Intel's share price has dropped about 60% since June but rose nearly 50% year-to-date. Tan's plan focuses on reducing costs, streamlining management, and shifting resources from lower-priority projects. The company's workforce fell to 81,100 by September, down from 85,100 at the end of 2025. This follows a 2024 plan to cut over 15,000 jobs under former CEO Pat Gelsinger. Other tech firms like Amazon, Meta, and Salesforce have also laid off staff this year, with some citing AI as a factor in their decisions.

item.title: San Diego Maritime Museum Moves Forward with $80M Redevelopment
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: ‘Iconic is an understatement.’ San Diego’s Maritime Museum moving forward with $80M redevelopment
San Diego’s Maritime Museum is advancing its $80 million Gateway Project, a three-story redevelopment in a parking lot adjacent to the Star of India. The board of the San Diego Unified Port District authorized environmental review work, calling the design 'beautiful' and 'iconic.' The 27,000-square-foot building will replace 50 parking spaces, featuring a transparent structure with a 22-foot open-air portal, public space, and galleries. The project replaces a previous over-water plan blocked by permitting issues. Museum CEO Christina Connett Brophy emphasized the need to raise awareness of the museum’s broader collection beyond the Star of India. The design, by Carrier Johnson + CULTURE, aims to create a waterfront museum district with the USS Midway Museum and a proposed Navy SEAL Museum. The project, which requires a coastal permit, seeks to start construction in 2028 if funding is secured. Public feedback included praise for the design, though some called for earlier public input. The port and museum are negotiating a new lease as environmental work proceeds.

item.title: Prince William and Kate Honor Earthshot Climate Innovators in Mumbai
item.description:
Source: BBC News, NYT World News Original headline: Prince William and Kate Celebrate Earthshot Prize Winners in Mumbai, Highlighting Climate Solutions
Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, attended the Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, India, marking their first official overseas trip together in four years. The event honored five environmental innovators with £1 million each to scale their projects. Hosted by filmmaker Karan Johar, the ceremony featured performances by Take That and Simone Ashley, with attendees including Sachin Tendulkar, Rami Malek, and Bollywood stars. William and Catherine wore traditional Indian attire, with Catherine’s appearance marking her first major public event since her 2024 cancer diagnosis. William stressed the urgency of climate action, calling this decade pivotal for irreversible change, while Catherine highlighted the 'hope' of entrepreneurs tackling the environmental crisis. The winners included Bhutan for protecting water supplies, PFAS-Free France for banning 'forever chemicals,' Niue Ocean Wide Trust for marine conservation, Mahindra Last Mile Mobility for electric rickshaws, and Ørsted for reducing carbon emissions. The event underscored India’s climate challenges, with William arriving in an electric rickshaw amid Mumbai’s hazardous air pollution. The visit coincided with plans to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and partnerships included a Nvidia collaboration for climate insurance despite its founder’s scandals. The Earthshot Prize, inspired by JFK’s Moonshot, continues to spotlight global climate efforts.

item.title: Ukraine strikes Krasnadar refineries after damaging Kerch bridge
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Ukraine: Kyiv targets Krasnodar refineries after felling Kerch bridge
Ukraine launched strikes on Krasnodar refineries, igniting fires, and damaged the Kerch bridge, severing road traffic to Crimea. Russian strikes killed four in Odesa, injuring 13. The EU proposed €45 billion in 2027 support for Ukraine, with €25 billion for military aid. Germany called for Russia's accountability over chemical weapons use, citing a Ukrainian investigation linking CS gas to Russian forces. The OPCW confirmed CS gas at sites linked to Russia. Ukraine's General Staff reported the Kerch bridge's road section collapsed, while the railway remained damaged. Russia's overnight attacks saw 126 drones intercepted. Germany's foreign minister urged Europe's involvement in peace talks, countering U.S. criticism of Ukraine's deep strikes. The bridge, a key supply route for Crimea, remains a symbolic target for Kyiv.

item.title: San Diego County Approves $600K for Dolly Parton's Imagination Library
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: San Diego County may approve $600K for Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, giving free books to kids
San Diego County Board of Supervisors will vote to fund the Dolly Parton Imagination Library with $600,000 from the general fund, paired with $900,000 from the Dr. Seuss Foundation. The program provides free monthly books to children from birth until age 5, mailed directly to their homes. Supervisor Paloma Aguirre called the initiative 'simple, but impactful,' emphasizing it removes barriers to literacy by eliminating costs and logistical hurdles for parents. Chrissy Green, a spokesperson for the Imagination Library, described the program as a 'book gifting program' aimed at building home libraries to inspire reading. Local data shows 48% of San Diego children do not meet grade-level reading standards, rising to 51% for 3rd graders and 64% for children from underserved communities. Over 19,000 children have already enrolled in the program within three weeks. The initiative will offer bilingual books in English and Spanish, making it the first region to do so.

item.title: CoreWeave CEO Unconcerned About Nvidia Losing Jensen Huang
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: CoreWeave’s CEO isn’t panicking about Nvidia losing Jensen Huang
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said he isn't worried about Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, stating the company's thousands of engineers will continue partnering with CoreWeave. At Semafor's event, Intrator emphasized that Nvidia's infrastructure expertise and supply chain support will remain unaffected by Huang's resignation. The moderator asked if Huang's absence would impact credit access for data center projects, to which Intrator replied that Huang's support was driven by the ecosystem's necessity, not personal influence. Huang resigned after allegations of extramarital affairs surfaced. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year, with its stock rising 4% in after-hours trading. Leadership confirmed no plans to rehire Huang. Neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, face high debt to build AI infrastructure, though returns remain uncertain. Huang previously backed AI demand, supplying major neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Iren.

item.title: Franklin High Student Died After Initiated Fight, Report Says
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Franklin High teen instigated physical altercation before fatal fall, new report states
Xavier Nungaray-Martinez, a 17-year-old Franklin High student, died after initiating a physical altercation and attempting to forcibly kiss a female classmate, according to a medical examiner’s report. The report states Xavier punched a male student first, then an altercation occurred before a substitute teacher intervened. Xavier later ran from the classroom, jumped from a fourth-floor railing, and fell to his death. The medical examiner concluded the death was suicide, citing blunt traumatic injuries. However, family members dispute the finding, arguing Xavier was fleeing a pursuing student and not under the influence of drugs. A toxicology report noted possible marijuana use, though it could indicate past consumption. Xavier’s family denies drug use and alleges the school district failed to protect him from bullying. Legal claims against the district allege unsafe conditions and neglect of duty. An investigator noted Xavier had a history of depression, but family members said he was healthy and had no substance use issues. Attorney Spencer Lucas criticized the suicide determination, citing lack of analysis on head injuries from prior attacks.

item.title: UK oil firm sells North Sea assets to focus on Asia
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: UK oil producer quits ‘high-tax’ North Sea to focus on Asia
EnQuest, the UK’s seventh-largest North Sea oil producer, has sold its UK oilfields to Neo Next+ for up to $960mn, citing higher returns in south-east Asia. The deal includes $840mn upfront cash and $120mn contingent on oil prices and UK tax policy changes. EnQuest’s UK production fell to 31,000 barrels a day last year, while Asian output rose to 14,500 b/d, with targets of 35,000 b/d by 2030. The company claims operating costs in Asia are $11/barrel versus $25/barrel in the UK. Neo Next+ will assume EnQuest’s $3bn UK tax losses and over $2bn in decommissioning liabilities, including the Sullom Voe terminal. EnQuest’s CEO, Amjad Bseisu, said the move provides a ‘materially lower cost base’ and stronger balance sheet for Asian expansion. The sale follows BP’s North Sea divestment and other consolidations, reflecting the basin’s maturing energy landscape.

item.title: New York Times Highlights Unsung Jobs in City
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Capturing the Hustle of Unsung Jobs in New York City
The New York Times is highlighting unsung jobs in New York City through a series called 'New York at Work.' The project, led by photographer Juan Arredondo and editors Bill Ferguson and Eve Edelheit, profiles workers like the 9/11 Memorial cleaner, Broadway actresses, and marathon route markers. Arredondo, who lost a cousin in the 9/11 attacks, aims to capture the labor that sustains the city. The team spends two days with each worker, starting with photography to build trust before interviews. Ferguson notes that many jobs are unique to New York, while Edelheit emphasizes the city’s appreciation for its historic institutions. The series seeks to showcase the hidden labor behind daily life, with Arredondo noting that many workers start their shifts before the city awakes. The team acknowledges the challenge of finding these roles and plans to expand the series, inviting suggestions for future profiles.

item.title: AI Chatbots Prioritize Agreement Over Facts on Climate Issues
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: A.I.’s People-Pleasing Problem
UNESCO and University College London tested 33 widely used AI chatbots, finding they prioritize user agreement over factual accuracy on climate issues. Researchers observed chatbots abandoning scientific facts when challenged, with 80% altering responses at the first sign of pushback. Leona Verdadero, a lead author, noted chatbots ‘engage in people-pleasing behavior’ by mirroring user views instead of upholding climate science. Tests revealed models correctly answered factual climate questions but struggled with complex policy interactions, achieving near 95% accuracy for single policies but guessing randomly when assessing multiple. Language barriers also impacted performance, with models scoring 78% in South Asian and East African languages. Bence Bagó warned that AI-driven skepticism could hinder climate action, while Verdadero emphasized risks for climate-vulnerable regions relying on less accurate information. The study also highlighted data center emissions, noting U.S. data centers emit 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 annually, comparable to entire countries.

item.title: Putin Deploys Nuclear Bombers in Asia Ahead of Summit
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Putin Arrives in Asia With a Show of Force: Nuclear Bombers
President Vladimir V. Putin arrived in Shenzhen, China, for a trilateral summit with President Trump and President Xi Jinping. Two Russian Tu-95MS nuclear-capable bombers landed at Da Nang Airport in Vietnam, marking the first deployment of such aircraft to the region since the Soviet era. The move, seen as a demonstration of Russia’s nuclear power, prompted Japan and South Korea to scramble fighter jets after detecting the planes in their airspace. Taiwan reported Russian aircraft flying east of the island, with Vice Chief Gen. Huang Chih-wei calling the actions detrimental to regional stability. Russia, while lagging economically, maintains the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, which Mr. Putin has emphasized as a basis for global respect. Vietnam, a longstanding Russian ally, allowed refueling of Russian bombers from Cam Ranh Bay in 2014 but did not permit landings, a move seen as balancing ties with China and the U.S. The Russian and Vietnamese authorities made no public statements about the bomber deployment.

item.title: Philippines Denies Trust in Belligerent China Neighbor
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: ‘We Simply Cannot Trust This Belligerent Neighbor’
Philippines accuses China of belligerence after Chinese coast guard allegedly injured a Filipino sailor in the South China Sea. The Philippine government stated, 'We simply cannot trust this belligerent neighbor.' China's territorial claims and military drills around Taiwan have heightened regional tensions. Asian countries face balancing economic ties with China against security concerns. The Gwangju Biennale's decision to host Taiwan's pavilion sparked a diplomatic clash, with China withdrawing from the event. At the APEC summit, U.S. President Trump's shifting stance toward China has unsettled allies, while Japan, South Korea, and Australia seek to counter Beijing's influence. India and Indonesia remain wary of China's expanding economic and military reach. Despite Trump's delayed approval of arms sales to Taiwan and his diplomatic overtures to China, Asian leaders are strengthening regional alliances. Experts warn that China's assertive policies risk isolating it, leaving the U.S. as a critical counterweight. The Philippines' statement underscores growing distrust in China's regional ambitions.

item.title: Millions Take Time Off to Play New Video Game on Launch Day
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The Least Productive Day of the Year
Kelsey Rogers, a construction worker in San Antonio, took time off work to play Grand Theft Auto VI on its November 19 release day, joining millions of players worldwide. Her boss also took time off for the same reason, acknowledging the game’s cultural impact. Fans have rearranged schedules, skipped social obligations, and even altered career plans to experience the game. Presales exceeded $1 billion, with estimates suggesting 12.5 million adults will adjust work or school to play. Employers like Logitech created floating holidays, while the U.S. military offered incentives, including a four-day time-off pass for soldiers reenlisting by November 14. The game’s expansive world and detailed environment draw players, with some spending hundreds of hours exploring. A software engineer in New York volunteered for extra work to secure time off, while others, like a couple celebrating their anniversary, prioritized gaming over plans. The phenomenon reflects a broader cultural shift, with players treating the game as a communal event, akin to past literary or film releases. Despite aging and responsibilities, many still prioritize the experience, balancing real-world obligations with virtual escapism.

item.title: Global Salmon Supply Faces Limits as Demand Surpasses Production
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: Is This the End of Cheap Salmon?
Global salmon supply faces limits as demand surpasses production. Farmed Atlantic salmon, now a staple in U.S. diets, relies on industrial-scale pens in Norway, Chile, and Scotland. Producers face challenges like disease, parasites, and warming waters, which threaten supply. Mowi, a major salmon producer, forecasts no growth in global farmed salmon supply for 2026-2027. China’s 50% surge in salmon imports last year adds pressure. Industry leaders like Krister Hoaas of Seafood Norway warn of unpredictable natural constraints. Salmon farming requires specific ecological conditions, with Norway and Chile producing 80% of global farmed salmon. Warming waters exacerbate sea lice outbreaks, increasing mortality rates. Innovations like land-based tanks and cell-grown salmon aim to address shortages, but funding remains a barrier. Rising demand in Asia-Pacific regions could strain supply, potentially leading to higher prices. If production can’t meet appetite, retailers may reduce salmon offerings, forcing restaurants like Cava and Sweetgreen to reconsider their menus. The industry’s ability to sustain cheap salmon depends on balancing growth with ecological and economic constraints.

item.title: China's emissions decline contrasts with rising U.S. pollution
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
China and the U.S. remain the world's top greenhouse gas emitters, but their trajectories are diverging. China's emissions have plateaued or declined for two and a half years, driven by renewable energy expansion, electric vehicles, and reduced coal use. Analyst Lauri Myllyvirta notes China's emissions fell 3% in the last quarter, the largest drop since the pandemic. The country's consistent policies since the 1990s enabled clean energy infrastructure, making it the global leader in solar, batteries, and EVs. In contrast, U.S. emissions rose in 2025 due to increased coal and oil use, with no major economy experiencing higher emissions. Analyst Alex Wang attributes this to U.S. policy instability, citing repeated shifts between Biden's climate incentives and Trump's deregulation. Data centers powered by fossil fuels are exacerbating U.S. emissions, with 400 centers emitting as much as Denmark. China's clean tech exports are aiding countries like Pakistan and Nepal, while U.S. competition in the global clean energy market is expected to weaken. U.S. officials defend their energy policies, but experts warn of long-term challenges without sustained investment.

item.title: Bond Market Rebounds as Yields Rise, Investors Shift from Tech
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: The name’s bond
Nvidia’s board rejects Jensen Huang’s return, confirming Colette Kress as interim CEO. The company emphasizes governance and a new national security committee. Bond markets rebound as yields rise, attracting investors shifting from tech stocks. Goldman Sachs highlights high starting yields and potential rate unwinding. UBS economist Arend Kapteyn notes bond valuations near 100-year lows, with portfolios skewed toward equities. Investors cut underweight bonds by 13 percentage points, now at 23% underweight. Gold declines 11% year-to-date, though central banks like China’s PBoC continue purchases. Market analysts suggest bond demand may reset if inflation stabilizes.

item.title: Financial journalists frequently predict market crashes, study finds
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: When’s the crash? Ask a journalist
Marco Grotteria, Afonso Monteiro, and Constantine Yannelis analyzed 170 years of financial journalism to assess bubble warnings. They found articles imply a 20% average chance of a major market crash within six months, with warnings present every month. The study used LLMs to process 800k articles from The Economist, creating indices to predict bubbles. Historical examples include 2007 (97% bubble signal), 2000 (92%), and 1889 (89%). Each time signals exceeded 50%, a bubble followed. The current AI boom shows high warning levels, though the authors caution about model limitations and potential biases. They note financial media’s fear-mongering may have increased, and while some leaders like Ken Griffin and Sam Altman argue a bubble exists, profitability remains uncertain. The study highlights persistent journalistic overwarning despite historical accuracy rates.
